title: Two Leaders

post.author: u/east_hall_walpurga
post.title: I keep the night book in a mountain commune's east hall. Snow shut the pass for three days. On the fourth morning, the closure our councillor wrote was gone from both books, and the road crew was already out.

blocks.text: Kesselwand is one commune, a self-governing village, in two valleys, with a council hall in each and the Hornjoch pass between them. Each hall keeps the whole commune book, our record of every standing decision, and takes decisions, so nobody has to climb the pass to ask. Every morning at 07:00 Fridolin, our runner, carries the west book over the pass and merges the two, bringing them into agreement. He does it in steps. He reads everything each book gained since his last crossing. Entries only one book has, he copies into the other. Where both halls wrote about the same matter, he follows the rule painted over both doors: where the books differ, the later entry stands. The other is struck, crossed out. I keep the east book at night.
On the first afternoon of the storm, snow shut the Hornjoch. For three days nothing crossed.

At 21:40 that night, by our clock, Councillor Gaudenz Imboden came in white to the knees and wrote the pass road CLOSED. He had heard the slope above the third bend settling. He walked down to the foot of the road himself and tied our red rag to the closure post.

On the fourth morning Fridolin came down with the west book and sat at my table to merge. His log, in his hand, is below. Each line shows when he merged, the matter, what each book said with the time its hall's clock gave it (d1 is day 1), and what he did:

Day 4, 07:00  pass road   east CLOSED 21:40 d1   west OPEN 21:44 d1      later: OPEN, CLOSED struck
Day 4, 07:00  woodpile    west two baskets 09:21 d2                    copied east
Day 4, 07:00  school      east SHUT 14:25 d2                           copied west
Day 4, 07:00  night bell  east HOURLY 18:02 d3   west MIDNIGHT 18:13 d3  later: MIDNIGHT, HOURLY struck
Day 4, 07:00  6 entries   4 kept   2 struck

The closure was struck from my book, in his hand. The west book never had it. The west book says Councillor Rosmarie Tschudin wrote the road OPEN at 21:44, to clear it for the supply cart. Gaudenz swears he wrote last. Her note, in Fridolin's bag, swears she did.
Two halls decided about the road that night. Neither book remembers the decision that came last.
By the time I had read it, the crew was clearing the third bend. I ran. The cart had already turned back: the carter had seen our red rag on the closure post, tied by a hand no book records.
Fridolin set his pocket watch against both clocks. Ours agreed with it. Theirs, the old pendulum in the west hall, was eleven minutes fast.
What should the council change before the next snow?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Each of your halls is what databases, the programs that keep records, call a leader: a copy that accepts writes, new entries, and passes them on to the other copies later. In the town-hall case there was one leader and the rest followed. Two halls that both take writes are multi-leader replication. It works in steps. Each leader writes into its own copy. Later it sends what it wrote to the other. At the merge, each copy takes in the other's changes. When both leaders change the same thing before either has heard from the other, that's a conflict, and something at the merge has to settle it. Your door rule is last writer wins: keep the entry with the later timestamp, the time its clock gave it, and drop the other. And when two clocks disagree about the time, the gap between them is clock skew. Now the log. By Fridolin's watch, which entry about the road was written first? What did the rule compare: the order things happened, or what each clock said? Of six entries, how many were struck, and who was told? And before the snow, whose job was the pass road?

replies.author: u/east_hall_walpurga
replies.text: Fridolin says the rule over the doors is older than either clock. The west clock is the old pendulum the sexton, the church caretaker, winds on Sundays; it gains a little every week, and nobody sets it. The road has always been the east hall's worry: our windows look straight at the third bend. The night bell is rung from the chapel, which serves both valleys.

comments.author: u/latest_wins_theodul
comments.text: Latest wins, last writer wins, is fair and simple. Whoever decided most recently knew the most, and nobody has to call a meeting over every disagreement. Your rule didn't fail; your clock did. Set both clocks by the church bell at noon and the later entry really is the later one. Every database I've run settles its conflicts this way, and I've never had a meeting about it.

comments.author: u/third_hall_pernille
comments.text: Two books can always end up one against one. Databases fix that with a quorum, enough copies agreeing for an answer to count. It works in steps. Keep each record in N copies. Send every write to all of them, and count it as done when W of them have it. Have each read ask R of them and take the newest answer. If R + W > N, the copies a read asks always include one the latest write reached, so it always sees it. Build a third hall by the chapel, write every decision to two of the three books, read two, and they can't disagree about what's latest.

reply.prompt: The next snow will come before the spring. What should the council of Kesselwand change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the rule that the later entry stands, but set both halls' clocks by the church bell at noon every single day.
options.part2: The sexton rang noon on Sunday and both clocks were set by it. By the first night of the next snow, in February, the west clock had gained a minute again, and the halls decided the same things at the same times as before. At the crossing on day 4, Fridolin's merge kept CLOSED at 21:40 over OPEN at 21:34, and struck Rosmarie's OPEN from the west book without a word. She had told the carter to be ready at first light, and nobody told her the road was shut. The night bell lost the east's HOURLY to MIDNIGHT at 18:03. Two entries struck, as before; this time a different pair. Gaudenz asked what would happen with the clocks exactly right. Fridolin worked it through on paper: the two bell entries were both written in the minute 18:02, and a tie goes to the east book, so one would still be struck.
options.senior: Setting the clocks shrinks the clock skew but never removes it, and the skew only decides which entry is lost. Last writer wins drops one of two writes every time two leaders change the same record, one entry, between merges, whatever the clocks say. And it drops it silently. The fix is to stop throwing a decision away, not to make the choice of which one look fairer.

options.text: Let no decision stand until both halls have signed it, so that the two books can never disagree about anything.
options.part2: The council voted that no entry stands until both halls have signed it. The next snow shut the Hornjoch for three days again. At 21:40 on the first night Gaudenz proposed the pass road CLOSED, and the book still said open, because the west hall hadn't signed. Six decisions waited in the bag: the closure, Rosmarie's cart, the woodpile, the school and both bells. The oldest waited 57 h 27 min. Not one was made while the pass was shut. For three days the book said the road was open, and Gaudenz tied the red rag on the post anyway, against the book. When Fridolin crossed on day 4, the two halls sat down to sign six decisions that had already been carried out or forgotten.
options.senior: Making every leader agree before a write counts turns two leaders back into one slow one. It removes conflicts by removing the ability to decide while cut off, which was the reason for having two halls. During a partition, when the copies are cut off from each other, nothing can be written anywhere. It suits rare decisions that can wait; it doesn't suit a commune that has to act while the pass is shut.

options.text: Give each matter one home hall that alone may change it; where books still differ, keep both for the council.
options.part2: The council gave each matter a home hall. The pass road and the school belong to the east, which watches the third bend and runs the school; the woodpile belongs to the west; the night bell, rung in the chapel for both valleys, has none. The next snow came in February. At 21:33 on the first night Rosmarie asked to open the road for the cart; the west book didn't change, and her request went in Fridolin's bag. At 21:40 Gaudenz wrote it CLOSED, and it stood. On day 4 Fridolin copied the closure west, the woodpile east and the school west, and wrote both bells, HOURLY and MIDNIGHT, into both books for the council. Nothing was struck. The council settled the bell in four minutes. Rosmarie's request reached the east hall after 57 h 27 min, and the east said no until the slope had been walked. The cart waited. The red rag on the post matched both books.
options.senior: Give each record one leader that alone may change it, and most conflicts can't happen; the cost is that a write from the wrong side waits for that leader, here 57 h 27 min. For records that truly belong to everyone, don't let a rule pick a winner silently: keep both versions and have a person, or the app's own merge, settle them. Nothing that matters is decided by a clock.

options.text: Build a third hall by the chapel; write each decision into two of the three books and read from two, so R + W > N.
options.verdict: Trade-off: only where it can reach
options.part2: The commune built a third hall beside the chapel, on the east side of the pass, and every decision went into two of the three books, with every reading taken from two. With the pass open it worked: any two books share at least one, so a reading always found the latest decision. Then the next snow shut the Hornjoch. The east hall reached its own book and the chapel's, two of three: its closure went in at 21:40 and stood. The west hall reached only its own, one of three, so its writes and its readings were refused for three days: no cart, no woodpile, no bell. Someone suggested writing the west's entries into a spare book, to hand over when the pass opened. That kept the west writing, but a reading of two books could then miss them.
options.senior: Quorums give a clean guarantee, R + W > N means every read overlaps the latest write, but only among the copies you can reach. A partition, a cut between the copies, leaves one side without a quorum, so it can't write at all, which is what two leaders were meant to avoid. A sloppy quorum, which counts stand-in copies like the spare book, keeps writes flowing and gives up the overlap. And quorums don't order two writes that arrive at once, so you still need a conflict rule.

sim.title: Run the Kesselwand books through the snow
sim.lede: You're Fridolin, replaying the snow from day 1, 07:00, just after your crossing. Snow shuts the Hornjoch at 13:00. Six entries follow, at the times your watch gives: the west's OPEN at 21:33 and the east's CLOSED at 21:40 on day 1, the woodpile at 09:10 and the school at 14:25 on day 2, and the east's HOURLY at 18:02:10 and the west's MIDNIGHT at 18:02:40 on day 3. Each book stamps an entry with its own clock, in whole minutes, and the west clock runs fast by the amount you set. You cross at 07:00 on the morning the pass reopens, and every morning after, merging what was written since. Pick the rule: latest entry wins (a tie goes to the east book, and the loser is struck without a word), keep both versions for the council, one home hall per matter (the east owns the pass road and the school, the west the woodpile, and the night bell has no home, so it keeps both), or both halls must sign every decision. Entries kept counts entries in the books after merging, two for a matter kept in two versions; a request or an unsigned proposal isn't kept. Part 2 has no leader: N books hold a record, a write waits for W of them and a read for R, and the worst read asks the R books furthest from the write's. Set how many books you can reach, and try a sloppy quorum, which writes to stand-in books outside the N when it can't reach W of its own. Changing a Part 1 setting replays from day 1, 07:00. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play to the end as now. OPEN at 21:44 beats CLOSED at 21:40 and the closure is struck from the east book; MIDNIGHT at 18:13 beats HOURLY: 4 kept, 2 struck. Set the west clock to 1 min fast: the closure stands, but OPEN is struck instead, still 2. At 0 min the bell's two entries share the minute 18:02 and one is still struck. Find where the pass road flips, between 7 and 8 min. Keep both versions: 6 kept, 2 for the council. One home hall: nothing struck, 1 for the council, and the west's OPEN waits 57 h 27 min as a request; shut the pass for 1 day and it waits 9 h 27 min. Both must sign: 6 waited, none decided in the snow. In Part 2, N 3, W 2 and R 2 share at least 1 book; drop W and R to 1 and the worst read misses. Set W and R back to 2 and reach 1 of 3: the write is refused. Turn on the sloppy quorum: accepted with 1 stand-in, and a read can miss it again.

explain.oneLine: Nothing erased the closure. Each hall was a leader, both decided about the pass road while cut off, and the merge kept the later stamp. The west clock ran 11 minutes fast, so OPEN, written 7 minutes before the closure, carried the later time, and the closure went into neither book.

steps.title: Two halls, two leaders.
steps.text: In leader-follower replication, as at the twin town halls, one copy takes every write and the others follow it. Kesselwand runs two leaders. That's multi-leader replication, and it works in steps. First each hall accepts decisions into its own book, without asking the other. Next Fridolin carries the changes over the pass; while the pass is shut, the changes wait, and the books drift apart. Then at the merge each book takes in the other's changes, and any matter both changed has to be settled. It suits sites that must keep working while cut off from each other: two valleys under snow, two regions of a database across an ocean (a region is a cloud company's group of data centers in one part of the world), or a phone with no signal. The phone is a leader for its own copy until it syncs, swapping changes with the server. The price is conflicts. If both leaders change the same record before either has heard from the other, the writes are concurrent: neither knew about the other, and nothing in the books says which should stand. The merge has to settle it. In three days of snow, two matters were changed on both sides: the pass road and the night bell.

steps.title: Latest wins throws one away, and the clock picks which.
steps.text: Last writer wins keeps the entry with the later timestamp, the time read from the writer's clock, and drops the other. It needs no person, which is why many databases use it by default. But it drops a write every time two leaders change the same record between merges, and it does so silently: Fridolin struck two of six entries and nobody was told. And 'later' is only as good as the clocks. By Fridolin's watch the west's OPEN was written at 21:33 and the east's CLOSED at 21:40, but the west clock ran 11 minutes fast, so OPEN carried 21:44 and won. Setting the clocks by the church bell shrinks the clock skew without removing it: a minute out, the closure survives but Rosmarie's OPEN is struck instead, and with the clocks exactly right the bell's two entries, both written in the minute 18:02, still lose one to the tie rule. Season 8 makes this Rule 6: never trust the clock on the wall.

steps.title: Three ways to keep every decision.
steps.text: Give each record one home leader that alone may change it, and a conflict on that record can't happen: the east hall owns the pass road, so the west's OPEN becomes a request that waits for the east. Where a record really belongs to everyone, keep both versions, called siblings, and let a person or the app's own merge settle them. Amazon's Dynamo, a database Amazon built for itself and described in a 2007 paper, did this for shopping carts. It merged two versions by keeping every item from both, so an added item is never lost, though a deleted one can come back. Or use a data type built to merge itself. A CRDT, short for conflict-free replicated data type, is a structure whose copies can be changed separately and always merged into the same result. A simple one is a counter where each copy keeps only its own count, and the total adds them up. CRDTs fit counts, sets and shared text; they can't decide whether a road is safe.

steps.title: No leader at all: quorums.
steps.text: Leaderless replication, the design of Dynamo, has no leader. Each record lives on N replicas, copies on different machines. A write works in steps. First it is sent to all N. Then it counts as done when W have saved it; a replica that is down or slow simply misses it. A read also works in steps. It asks R replicas, then takes the newest version any of them has; a replica that missed the write answers with an old one. If R + W > N, any R replicas include at least one of the W the write reached, so a read sees the latest write. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2, any two books share one. W = 1 and R = 1 make reads and writes faster, but a read can ask the one book the write missed. Cassandra, another leaderless database, calls the choice a consistency level: QUORUM is a majority, so QUORUM writes and QUORUM reads overlap. Replicas that missed a write catch up two ways. A read that finds a stale, out-of-date copy can fix it on the spot, which is read repair. And a background job compares replicas and copies what differs, which is anti-entropy. Merkle trees make that cheaper: trees of short fingerprints of the data, called hashes, so two replicas can find their differences by comparing a few fingerprints.

steps.title: What quorums don't promise.
steps.text: The overlap holds only among replicas you can reach. Put a third hall by the chapel and the snow still leaves the west hall with one book of three: it can't get W = 2 for a write or R = 2 for a read, so it stops. Dynamo keeps writing through a sloppy quorum, in steps. It writes to the first N healthy nodes, the machines that answer, using stand-ins for the unreachable ones. A stand-in keeps the write with a note of where it belongs. When that replica is back, the stand-in hands the write over, which is hinted handoff. Writes stay possible, but a read can now miss them. Quorums also don't order two writes that arrive at once: Dynamo keeps both as versions, and Cassandra settles them by last write wins on timestamps, so the clock question comes back. On many systems a read that overlaps a write still in progress can see the new value, and the next read the old one.

fix.title: The fix: one home hall per matter, and both versions for the council
fix.text: Give every matter a home hall that alone may change it: the pass road and the school to the east, the woodpile to the west. A hall that wants to change a matter it doesn't own sends a request with Fridolin, and the home hall decides. Matters with no natural home, like the night bell, keep both versions when the books differ, and the council settles them. Paint over the old rule: the merge never strikes an entry. In the sim, the same three days under this rule end with 5 entries kept, none struck, one matter with two versions for the council, and one request that waited 57 h 27 min. Keep the clocks set, too, but only so the stamps are readable; nothing is decided by them.

limits: A home hall makes the other side wait. Rosmarie's request took 57 h 27 min to reach the east, and a matter whose home hall is cut off can't change at all. Choose homes by who must decide, and accept that some decisions wait.
Keeping both versions only moves the conflict to a person or to code. Someone has to settle them, and a merge that keeps everything from both, like Dynamo's cart, can bring back what was deleted.
Neither helps with a number both halls must change while cut off, such as a shared count. That needs a CRDT, a data type built to merge itself, or one hall that owns it.

explain.seniorTake: Several leaders buy you writes that keep working while sites are cut off, and the bill is conflicts. Decide how each kind of record settles them before you need to. First, make conflicts impossible where you can: give each record one home leader, by user, by region or by owner. Where you can't, never let a timestamp silently pick a winner for anything that matters. Keep both versions for a person or a merge, or model the data as a CRDT, a type that merges itself. Treat last writer wins as a choice for data you can afford to lose, like a session, a user's short-lived login state, not a default. And when someone offers quorums, ask what happens on the side of a partition, a cut between copies, that can't reach a majority.

realWorld.title: Amazon Dynamo, 2007: always writeable
realWorld.text: DeCandia and colleagues say Dynamo is targeted mainly at applications that need an always writeable data store where no updates are rejected due to failures or concurrent writes. The shopping cart is the example: an Add to Cart operation can never be forgotten or rejected. Taking writes everywhere is what makes conflicts certain.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: R + W > N, usually (3,2,2)
realWorld.text: R is the minimum number of nodes, machines holding copies, that must participate in a successful read operation and W the same for writes, and the paper says setting R and W such that R + W > N yields a quorum-like system. Because a get or put, a read or write, waits for the slowest of its R or W replicas, R and W are usually configured to be less than N. The common (N,R,W) configuration used by several instances of Dynamo is (3,2,2).

realWorld.title: Dynamo: the sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
realWorld.text: A traditional quorum, the paper says, would be unavailable during server failures and network partitions. So Dynamo does not enforce strict quorum membership and instead uses a sloppy quorum: all read and write operations are performed on the first N healthy nodes from the preference list, the ordered list of machines responsible for each key. Hinted handoff then ensures that the read and write operations are not failed due to temporary node or network failures.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: two ways to settle versions
realWorld.text: Some services use business logic specific reconciliation, where the client application performs its own reconciliation; the shopping cart merges different versions of a customer's cart, so an add to cart is never lost, though the paper adds that deleted items can resurface. Others use timestamp based reconciliation, last write wins, where the object with the largest physical timestamp value is chosen; the example is the service that maintains customer session information.

realWorld.title: Dynamo: read repair and anti-entropy
realWorld.text: When a read gets stale versions back, the coordinator, the node handling that read, updates those nodes with the latest version, which the paper calls read repair. For replicas that drift further, an anti-entropy protocol compares Merkle trees, hash trees whose leaves are hashes of the values of individual keys, so two nodes can find their differences without sending everything.

realWorld.title: Apache Cassandra: consistency levels
realWorld.text: Cassandra's documentation lists the levels: ONE, only a single replica must respond; QUORUM, a majority (n/2 + 1) of the replicas; ALL, all of the replicas; LOCAL_QUORUM, a majority in the local datacenter. Write operations are always sent to all replicas, and the level controls how many responses the coordinator, the node handling the request, waits for. It is common, the page says, to pick levels so that W + R > RF, the replication factor, Cassandra's name for N: if QUORUM is used for both writes and reads, at least one of the replicas is guaranteed to participate in both.

realWorld.title: Apache Cassandra: last write wins, and the clocks
realWorld.text: Every mutation enters with a timestamp, from the client's clock or the coordinator node's, and updates resolve according to the conflict resolution rule of last write wins, separately for each column. The documentation is direct about the cost: Cassandra's correctness does depend on these clocks, so make sure a proper time synchronization process is running such as NTP. NTP, the Network Time Protocol, is the usual way computers set their clocks over the network.

realWorld.title: Riak: siblings
realWorld.text: Riak's documentation says a sibling is created when Riak is unable to resolve the canonical version of an object, for example after concurrent writes, and recommends allowing Riak to generate siblings and designing your application to resolve conflicts where its built-in data types don't fit. Of resolving by timestamps it warns that they are not a reliable resolution mechanism in distributed systems, and they always bear the risk of data loss.

realWorld.title: CRDTs
realWorld.text: crdt.tech describes optimistic replication, where users may modify the data on any replica independently of any other replica, even if the replica is offline, and says CRDTs ensure that, no matter what data modifications are made on different replicas, the data can always be merged into a consistent state, automatically. It points to Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski's 2011 study as the older reference.

realWorld.title: Amazon DynamoDB global tables
realWorld.text: AWS's DynamoDB guide notes that global tables, copies of a table in several regions that each take writes, use last writer wins between concurrent updates, so its version-number check, which refuses a write if the record changed since you read it, does not work as expected there. A multi-region, active-active database can carry Kesselwand's door rule by default.

asked: How do you handle write conflicts across regions?
interview.answer: Start with why you have several leaders: each region or device must take writes while cut off, so conflicts will happen and need a plan. First avoid them. Give each record a home region or owner that alone takes its writes, and route writes there. Where that isn't possible, settle conflicts deliberately. Keep both versions for the app or a person to merge, or use CRDTs, data types that merge themselves, for counters, sets and text. Last writer wins is dangerous because it silently drops one of two concurrent writes, writes made without knowing of each other. And it orders them by clocks that drift, so the write it keeps may not be the last. Reserve it for data you can afford to lose. For R + W > N: each record lives on N replicas. A write waits for W of them to confirm, and a read waits for R answers. If R + W > N, any set of replicas a read asks overlaps any set a write reached, so a read sees the latest confirmed write. N = 3 with W = 2 and R = 2 is common. Then name the limits. The overlap holds only among replicas you can reach, so a partition, a network cut, can leave one side unable to write. A sloppy quorum, writing to stand-ins and handing the writes back later (hinted handoff), keeps writing but gives up the overlap. And quorums don't order concurrent writes, so you still need a conflict rule. Read repair, fixing stale copies when a read finds them, and anti-entropy, a background comparison made cheap with Merkle trees, bring stale replicas back in line.

terms.def: A village or group of villages that governs itself. Kesselwand is one commune in two valleys.
Where a valley's councillors meet and write decisions into the commune book. Kesselwand has one in each valley, east and west.
An elected member of the commune's council. Gaudenz Imboden sits in the east hall, Rosmarie Tschudin in the west.
Kesselwand's record of every standing decision, kept whole in each hall.
The only way between Kesselwand's two valleys. Snow shut it for three days.
Fridolin, who carries the west book over the pass every morning at 07:00 and merges the two books.
Fridolin's job at each crossing: compare everything written since the last one, copy single entries across, and settle any matter both halls changed.
Crossed out of a book at the merge because the other hall's entry won. Nobody is told.
A post at the foot of the pass road where the east hall ties a red rag when the road is closed.
The church caretaker, who winds the west hall's clock on Sundays and rings the bell at noon.
A copy of the data that accepts writes and passes them on to the other copies. Each Kesselwand hall is a leader for the commune book.
A copy that takes no writes of its own and applies the changes its leader sends.
One leader takes every write and the followers apply its changes, so there is only ever one place a record can change.
Several leaders each accept writes and send them to the others later, so each site keeps working while cut off. Conflicts are the price.
A setup where two or more sites, such as two regions, all take writes at once. Multi-leader replication across regions is one.
Two leaders change the same record before either has heard from the other, so the merge finds two different values and must settle them.
Writes made without knowledge of each other. Neither came after the other in any sense the system can see, whatever their clocks say.
How far two clocks disagree at the same moment. The west hall's clock is 11 minutes ahead of the east's.
The time recorded with a write, read from some machine's clock. Last writer wins compares these, so it trusts that clock.
The time a hall's clock gives an entry, in whole minutes. Latest wins compares stamps, not the real order.
What latest wins does with two equal stamps. In the sim the east book's entry stands and the west's is struck.
Two or more versions of one record kept side by side after a conflict, for a person or the app to merge. Riak's word for them.
The one leader allowed to change a given record, so it can't conflict. Kesselwand's home halls: the east for the pass road and school, the west for the woodpile.
A change asked for by a hall that doesn't own the matter. It goes in Fridolin's bag and the home hall decides at the next crossing.
Under the both-halls-sign rule, an entry that changes nothing until the other hall signs it at a crossing.
Conflict-free replicated data type: a structure whose copies can be changed separately and always merge to the same result, such as a counter that adds each copy's own count.
A simple CRDT: each copy counts only its own additions, and the total is the sum of every copy's count, so merges never lose one.
Letting any copy be changed on its own, even offline, and settling differences when copies meet. crdt.tech's name for it.
No copy is the leader: a write goes to several replicas, the copies, directly, and a read asks several, as in Amazon's Dynamo and Cassandra.
The number of replicas that must answer for a read or write to count, such as two of three.
N: how many replicas hold a record. W: how many must have a write before it counts. R: how many a read asks. Dynamo's usual is 3, 2, 2.
If the replicas a read asks plus those a write reached add up to more than N, they must share at least one, so the read sees the write.
The read that asks the R books furthest from the ones the write reached. If even it overlaps, every read does.
When a record's own replicas can't be reached, counting writes on the first healthy stand-ins instead. Writes keep working; R + W > N no longer guarantees overlap.
In the sim, a book outside the N that holds a write for a cut-off book under a sloppy quorum, to hand back later.
A stand-in replica keeps a write with a note of which replica it was meant for, and hands it over when that replica is back.
In Dynamo, the ordered list of machines responsible for a record. Reads and writes go to the first N healthy ones on it.
When a read finds a replica with an old version, sending it the newest one on the spot.
A background job that compares replicas and copies across whatever differs, so even rarely read records catch up. Like two clerks checking their books page by page.
A tree of hashes, short fingerprints of data: each leaf fingerprints one record and each branch fingerprints the ones below it, so two replicas find their differences by comparing a few.
The machine that takes a program's read or write, passes it to the replicas, then waits for enough of them to answer, like a clerk collecting signatures.
Cassandra's setting for how many replicas must answer a read or write, such as ONE, QUORUM or ALL.
Cassandra consistency levels: one replica must respond, a majority (n/2 + 1) must, or all of them must.
A Cassandra consistency level: a majority of the replicas in the coordinator's own datacenter must respond.
Cassandra's name for a group of its machines in one place, such as one cloud region. One Cassandra system can span several.
Cassandra's name for N: how many replicas hold each piece of data.
Cassandra's word for a write: an insert, update or delete, carrying a timestamp.
Amazon's in-house database that finds each value by its key, like a cloakroom ticket. Described in a 2007 paper: leaderless, always takes writes, uses quorums and lets the app merge versions.
Dynamo's word for settling different versions of one object into one, either by the app's own logic or by last write wins.
A list of counters, one per machine, kept with each version so a system can tell whether one version came after another or the two were made without knowing of each other.
A free database that finds each value by its key, and can keep conflicting versions of a record side by side as siblings.
An app designed to work fully without a connection, keeping its own copy and syncing later. Each device is in effect a leader.
Never trust the clock on the wall. One of the seven rules; Season 8 teaches it.

atWork: Look for places in your systems where two copies can take writes to the same record while apart. Offline-first mobile apps, built to work with no signal, are the usual one: every phone is a leader for its own copy until it syncs. Multi-region, active-active databases, where every region takes writes, are the other. One is DynamoDB global tables, Amazon's rented database copied across regions, which settle concurrent updates by last writer wins. A common bug looks like this: a calendar app syncs edits by keeping the copy with the newest timestamp, a user moves a meeting on their phone on the train and renames it on their laptop, and after both sync one of the two edits has quietly gone. For each such record, ask three questions. Can two sites change it while apart, or does it have one home that alone takes its writes? When two versions meet, what happens: does a timestamp silently pick one, are both kept for the user or the app, or is it a type that merges itself, such as a counter or a set? And whose clock does the timestamp come from? If you run quorum reads and writes, write down N, W and R for each table and check R + W > N where reads must see the latest write, then ask what one side of a network partition, a cut between the copies, can still do. If your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report, an auditor's report on its controls, that includes the processing integrity category, its criteria (PI1.3 in the AICPA's 2017 Trust Services Criteria) expect data to be processed completely and accurately; a write dropped without trace by a merge rule is the kind of gap an auditor can ask about, so decide each record's conflict rule now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's notes app works offline on phones and laptops and syncs to a server later. A user edits a shopping list on the train with no signal, then edits the same list on her laptop at home. After both sync, the train edit has vanished. The server keeps whichever copy has the newest device timestamp. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Both copies changed the same list concurrently, and last-writer-wins kept one and silently dropped the other
Device clocks disagree, so the newest-looking timestamp isn't necessarily the last edit
Keep both versions for the user, or merge them by meaning: per item, or with a CRDT

recall.model: Both devices were leaders for the same list while apart, so their edits were concurrent, and the server's last-writer-wins rule kept one copy and silently dropped the other. Which one it kept depended on the device clocks, and a phone's clock can be minutes off, so the newest-looking timestamp isn't even necessarily the last edit. Don't settle it by timestamp. Keep both versions when they conflict and show both to the user, or merge them by meaning: a shopping list is a set of items, so merge per item, or use a CRDT that merges list edits automatically. Never drop a user's edit without telling them.

recall.prompt: A store keeps each key on N = 3 replicas. Which setting makes every read overlap at least one replica that the latest successful write reached?
recall.why: A read is sure to overlap a write only if R + W > N. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2 add up to 4, so any two replicas the read asks share at least one with the two the write reached. The other three add up to 2 or 3, so a read can ask only replicas the write never reached. Dynamo's common setting was this one, (3,2,2).

recall.prompt: Your company runs its customer database active-active in two regions, far-apart groups of data centers, and either region can take any write. A customer's delivery address and an account's 'closed' flag can each be changed in both regions within the same second. How would you handle write conflicts, and why not just keep the newest write?

keyIdeas.idea: Give each customer or account a home region that alone takes its writes, so conflicts can't happen
Last-writer-wins silently drops one of two writes, and clock skew decides which
Where a record can't have one home, keep both versions for a person or a merge, or use a CRDT

recall.model: Give each customer a home region that alone takes writes to their records, and route writes there; then two regions can't change the same record at once, at the cost of a slower write when the user is far from home, or none while the home region is cut off. Don't keep the newest write: last-writer-wins silently drops the other one, and with clock skew between regions it may drop the one that really came last. For anything that can't have one home, keep both versions when they conflict and let a person or a merge function settle them, per field where the fields are independent, or model it as a CRDT. A closed flag set in one region should never vanish because an address change elsewhere carried a later timestamp.

recall.prompt: Dynamo uses a sloppy quorum: when some of a key's own replicas can't be reached, reads and writes go to the first N healthy nodes instead. What does that give up?
options: Writes: any write is refused while one of the key's replicas is down
The promise that, with R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest write
Durability: a write held by a stand-in node is never handed back
Nothing: it is as strong as a strict quorum, and only faster
recall.why: A sloppy quorum keeps writes working through failures and partitions by counting stand-in nodes, and hinted handoff later hands each write to the replica it was meant for. Until then, the W nodes that took a write may not include any of the R a read asks, even with R + W > N, so the overlap guarantee is gone. Refusing writes is what a strict quorum would do.

recall.prompt: According to Apache Cassandra's documentation, how does Cassandra settle two concurrent updates to the same column?
options: Last write wins, by the mutation's timestamp
It returns every conflicting value to the client
The coordinator asks a majority of replicas to vote
A vector clock picks the update that came later
recall.why: Cassandra's documentation says every mutation carries a timestamp, from the client or the coordinator node's clock, and updates resolve by last write wins, per column. It adds that Cassandra's correctness depends on these clocks, so a time synchronization process such as NTP must run. Dynamo and Riak, by contrast, can keep conflicting versions for the application.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The home halls work; the closure post and both books have agreed all spring. But in April the council started counting the firewood baskets taken from the commune's winter store, which both valleys draw from, so the count has no home. The pass was shut for two days. The book said 120 taken before it. The east hall wrote the count up to 141, the west to 137. Both went to the council as two versions, and the council kept the larger, 141. When they counted the store in May, it was 17 baskets lighter than the book says.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are 17 baskets missing from the book, and how should the count be kept?

keyIdeas.idea: Each version holds only one hall's takings; choosing either loses the other hall's, so they need adding, not choosing
Keep a separate count per hall and take the total as their sum: a grow-only counter, a CRDT
Record what each hall took, the change, rather than overwriting a total

coldCase.model: Both versions were right, and neither was the answer. Starting from 120, the east took 21 baskets and the west 17, so the true count is 158; keeping either version, 141 or 137, throws away the other hall's takings, and the council's pick lost the west's 17. A count that both sides change while apart needs adding, not choosing. Record what each hall took, the change, not a new total, and keep a separate count per hall: the total is the sum of every hall's own count, and a merge just takes each hall's latest own count. That's a grow-only counter, one of the simplest CRDTs, the data types built to merge themselves, and it merges the same way whatever order the books meet in.

sources.title: Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani and others, Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store, SOSP 2007 (always writeable, no updates rejected due to failures or concurrent writes; R + W > N yields a quorum-like system; R and W usually less than N; sloppy quorum on the first N healthy nodes and hinted handoff; business logic specific and timestamp based reconciliation; deleted items can resurface; read repair; anti-entropy with Merkle trees; the common (N,R,W) configuration (3,2,2))

Apache Cassandra Documentation (stable), Architecture: Dynamo (tunable consistency levels ONE, TWO, THREE, QUORUM, ALL, LOCAL_QUORUM, EACH_QUORUM, LOCAL_ONE, ANY; writes always sent to all replicas; W + R > RF; QUORUM for both guarantees overlap; mutation timestamps and last write wins per column; correctness depends on clocks, run NTP; read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy repair with Merkle trees)

crdt.tech, About CRDTs, maintained by Martin Kleppmann, Annette Bieniusa and Marc Shapiro (optimistic replication; CRDTs ensure the data can always be merged into a consistent state, automatically; cites Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski, A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types, 2011)

Riak KV Documentation: Conflict Resolution (siblings are created when Riak can't resolve the canonical version, for example after concurrent writes; allow siblings and resolve conflicts in the application; timestamps are not a reliable resolution mechanism and always bear the risk of data loss)
Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: DynamoDB and optimistic locking with version number (global tables use last writer wins between concurrent updates)
AICPA & CIMA: 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022) (the criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality and Privacy used in SOC 2 reports)
Linford & Co: What is Processing Integrity and Who Needs it in their SOC 2? (PI1.3, data is processed completely, accurately, and timely as authorized; processing integrity is optional)
